{"id": "1:2/q11", "question": "How is al-ʿālamīn formed and derived?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿālam is a sign, a means of knowledge, or a collective; how its sound plural is justified.", "positions": [{"id": "1:2/q11/p1", "position": "ʿĀlam derives from a sign pointing to the Creator.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj derives ʿālam from knowledge or a sign because the world points to its maker; ʿālamīn encompasses all beings besides God, including human and jinn realms. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Al-ʿālamīn denotes what makes the Creator known—bodies, substances, and accidents—or every existent apart from God; its sound masculine plural reflects a descriptive quality associated with rational beings. QASHANI, d. 736 (author): God is Lord of the worlds as origin, preserver, and manager of all; worlds means everything known to God, and the sound masculine plural reflects encompassing knowledge or predominance. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): Al-alamin is an annexed sound masculine plural in form but an ism-jam because its singular differs; it cannot be plural of alam if that covers all non-divine beings while al-alamin means rational beings only. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): Sibawayh similarly says a'rab is not plural of arab because the former is narrower; an objection that al-alamin could mean only rational alam is answered by comparison with the unavailable form shay'un. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعضهم): Some commentators restrict the worlds to beings with knowledge: angels and the two accountable species, humans and jinn. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The sound plural al-alamin foregrounds rational beings; a concise Turkish rendering is difficult, but it means God alone is Lord of all realms and especially their rational inhabitants. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The sound rational plural and the definite article extend the meaning across all realms and foreground rational beings; understanding the Lord of the worlds requires conceiving rational agents. IBNASHUR, d. 1393 (author): The plural uses the rational masculine form even though some worlds are nonrational, by giving precedence to rational beings. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (author): This plural suits al-Fatiha because its worship, aid, guidance, and moral categories address accountable creatures; Rabb al-alamin may mean their Lord or all creation with rational beings predominant. ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 (author): The article in al-ʿālamīn is exhaustive; ʿālam is an irregular collective and its sound masculine plural is even more irregular because it violates some conditions of that pattern. ALUSI, d. 1270 (author): The suggestion that ʿālamīn is a unique collective noun on the pattern of sound plurals does not settle its form; the author distinguishes ordinary plurals, collective generics, and collective nouns. IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, encompassing every created being besides God; created kinds in heavens, earth, land, and sea are worlds, as is each generation.
